summary: Lecture 9 is the basics scaling-law lecture; Lecture 10 is inference and Lecture 11 returns to advanced scaling topics.
Scaling laws are small-scale predictive rules used to extrapolate large-scale behavior.
Scaling-style learning curves predate modern LLMs; Hestness 2017 showed broad neural power-law trends.
E(x) ≈ A x^{-α}; log E ≈ log A - α log x.
For x_i~N(mu,sigma^2), sample-mean MSE is E[(mu_hat-mu)^2]=sigma^2/n.
Neural data-scaling exponents are often O(0.1–0.3), much slower than 1/n; n^{-1/d} gives a nonparametric intuition.
Data composition and mixture ratio can be modeled; the best mixture need not be treated as scale-independent.
Repeated data yields diminishing effective-data gains rather than linearly equivalent fresh data.
Data filtering policy changes with scale because additional data must often come from lower-quality regions.
Compare architecture scaling curves at small compute rather than training a frontier-scale candidate directly.
Look for scale-invariant hyperparameters whose optimum is stable across model sizes.
Parameter counting is a modeling choice; embedding/non-embedding definitions can change apparent scaling regularity.
MoE scaling must distinguish total parameters, active parameters, compute and sparsity.
Critical batch size marks the crossover from near-ideal variance-reduction gains to diminishing returns.
S/S_min - 1 = (E/E_min - 1)^(-1), with B_crit=E_min/S_min.
The critical batch size increases predictably as target loss improves; it can itself be fit as a scaling law.
Two LR strategies: extrapolate the moving optimum across scale, or reparameterize (e.g. μP) to make the optimum transfer.
Upstream loss/perplexity scaling can be clean while downstream rankings differ; transfer must be validated separately.
Before a large run, scaling experiments should predict the expected loss and approximate gains from recipe choices.
At fixed training compute, model size N and data D trade off; joint L(N,D) models can be fit and optimized under a FLOPs constraint.
Kaplan favored faster parameter growth; Chinchilla shifted toward roughly balanced growth and the familiar ~20 tokens/parameter training-compute rule.
Chinchilla uses three methods: minima over training curves, IsoFLOP profiles, and parametric loss modeling.
Small recipe details—parameter counting, warmup and batch size—can materially shift the inferred scaling law.
A scaling law predicts what happens if the current recipe is scaled; a bad small-scale recipe can be faithfully extrapolated.
Later refitting of Chinchilla method 3 suggested the original surface fit underfit the data; the refit aligned much better with methods 1/2.
Training-compute optimum is not deployment optimum; serving-heavy systems may rationally use many more tokens per parameter.
IsoFLOP fixes a compute budget and sweeps remaining degrees of freedom; it is a robust default experimental design.
Scaling regularities enable evidence-driven engineering at scale without repeatedly running frontier-size experiments.
